sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Can large language model (LLM) agents deliver expert-level operations research (OR) solutions directly from original client materials, without prior expert reformulation? Existing OR benchmarks typically begin with self-contained descriptions or predefined optimization tasks, underrepresenting the translation of original business materials into professionally validated solutions. We introduce OR-License, an end-to-end benchmark of 31 instances across 10 industrial scenarios from paid OR engagements totaling USD 3.68 million. It preserves original requirements, input data, deliverable formats, and information boundaries after de-identification. To study information acquisition, we introduce ORSim, a controlled client simulator that discloses business facts without supplying OR expertise. Hidden evaluation checks feasibility and compares objective quality against original expert solutions accepted by clients before benchmark construction. Deployment-Adjusted Quality (DAQ) averages expert-relative quality across instances, assigning zero to infeasible deliveries. Across 11 frontier LLMs using coding-agent harnesses, several exceed the expert reference in conditional objective quality, but none matches its DAQ; the strongest primary Claude Code configuration achieves 88.39% strict feasibility and a DAQ of 0.87 against the expert reference of 1. Client information acquisition extends beyond clarification into solution development and validation, with some later stages showing higher confirmed issue-resolution proportions. Trajectory analysis identifies formulation and implementation failures, while task-equalized research-chain completion rates range from 24% to 45% across models on evaluable tasks. These findings motivate sustained information-gap resolution, faithful problem formulation, and evidence-linked self-improvement for reliable long-horizon agents.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Operations research (OR) supports high-value decisions across manufacturing, logistics, healthcare, retail, and many other domains. Deploying an OR system, however, requires experts to transform incomplete business materials into an executable decision process through requirement elicitation, problem formulation, solution strategy selection, and solver implementation. Gurobis State of Mathematical Optimization Report 2024 reports that 82% of survey respondents hold masters or doctoral degree (Gurobi Optimization, 2024). We ask whether large language model (LLM) agents can carry out this work. Equal contribution. Correspondence to: Yong-Hong Kuo<yhkuo@hku.hk> and Jia Li<jialee@hkust-gz.edu.cn>. 1 OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners Figure 1: Three gaps and corresponding improvements in OR-LICENSE. Each column links an evaluation gap (top) to its improvement (bottom). The client dialogue is illustrative. Recent work has explored LLMs for OR (Ramamonjison et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025; AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026), with newer benchmarks extending evaluation to multi-stage agent workflows (Zhou et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a). However, three important gaps remain in evaluating whether LLMs can take on the work of OR experts in real-world engagements. Gap 1: Task Complexity and Practical Relevance. Benchmarks built from academic, synthetic, or reconstructed tasks may not capture the operational complexity and practical demands of real client engagements, limiting what their results reveal about LLMs ability to perform professional OR work. Gap 2: Information Acquisition. Evaluations that provide the full task context omit the work required to establish that context, limitation explicitly acknowledged by GDPval (Patwardhan et al., 2025). In real OR engagements, practitioners must identify missing client-held information, ask targeted questions, and integrate the answers throughout problem solving. Gap 3: Limited Grounding in Professional Delivery. Professional OR capability requires reference grounded in the solution quality achieved by experts in real client engagements, alongside correctness checks and algorithmic baselines. Evaluation-specific references can validate task criteria, whereas client-accepted expert deliveries anchor the comparison in outcomes that satisfied real client requirements. As illustrated in Figure 1, to address these gaps, we introduce OR-LICENSE, an end-to-end benchmark built from real-world OR engagements. The name reflects our focus on the skills required in professional OR practice. OR-LICENSE comprises three core improvements: First, we ground evaluation in original paid industrial OR engagements, preserving realistic requirements, artifacts, and ambiguity after de-identification. Second, we introduce ORSIM, which lets agents acquire client-side business information throughout the workflow while maintaining boundary between customer knowledge and OR expertise. Third, we evaluate agents against original expert solutions 2 OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners that were accepted by clients before benchmark construction, providing realistic reference for professional-quality delivery. We use OR-LICENSE to investigate three research questions: RQ1: How do LLM agents compare with OR experts in feasibility and objective quality, and how consistently do they complete evidence-grounded investigations? RQ2: When do agents acquire client information across the OR workflow, and how does it contribute to confirmed issue resolution? RQ3: What failure patterns emerge when agents translate business requirements into executable OR solutions, and what capability gaps do they reveal? The contributions of this work are threefold: dataset grounded in paid industrial OR engagements. We curate and release 31 instances across 10 industries, derived from commissioned OR projects representing $3.68 million in total project value (Section 3.2). An end-to-end evaluation framework for LLM agents as OR practitioners. We formalize the OR workflow from requirement elicitation to executable decision making and introduce ORSIM, controlled client simulator that provides business facts throughout formulation, solving, and refinement without supplying OR expertise. We integrate this interaction with coding-agent harnesses and hidden post-submission evaluation of feasibility and expert-relative solution quality (Sections 3.1 and 4). Deployment-oriented metrics and trajectory analysis. We introduce Deployment-Adjusted Quality (DAQ), averaging expert-relative quality with zero credit for infeasible deliveries, and ReliabilityQuality Profile. Across eleven frontier LLMs, we analyze client information acquisition, failure patterns, and linked cycles of hypothesis formation, experimentation, and revision to relate observed inquiry to delivery performance (Sections 3.4 and 4).

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: LLMs for Operations Research. OptiMUS uses modular agent for mathematical formulation, solver-code generation, and execution-based revision (AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024). ORLM, ReSocratic, and OptMATH improve optimization modeling through specialized training and data synthesis (Huang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025), while ARS generates constraint-aware heuristic code for vehicle-routing variants (Li et al., 2025). Many existing evaluations begin with self-contained problem descriptions or predefined optimization tasks (Ramamonjison et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025). OR-Space and ORAgentBench extend evaluation to multi-file executable environments and multi-stage workflows (Zhou et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a). OR-LICENSE builds on this direction using original materials from paid industrial engagements, preserving their requirements, data formats, ambiguity, terminology, and information boundaries after de-identification. Agents can query ORSIM throughout formulation, solving, and refinement, making client interaction part of building the executable solution. Benchmarking LLMs for Professional Work. Recent benchmarks such as GDPval, APEX-Agents, and AgencyBench evaluate economically valuable deliverables and sustained execution across professional tasks and realistic scenarios (Patwardhan et al., 2025; Vidgen et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b). OR-LICENSE specializes this direction to OR: executable submissions are checked for feasibility against original client requirements, and objective quality is assessed relative to original expert solutions accepted by clients before benchmark construction. Table 8 summarizes the comparison. 3 OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners Figure 2: The OR-LICENSE evaluation framework. Experts curate tasks and reference solutions from real-world OR projects. Agents may query ORSIM throughout problem solving. Final submissions undergo hidden evaluation of feasibility and expert-relative solution quality.

(a): The two-ring donut summarizes the covered industries (outer ring) and OR problem types (inner ring). Industry categories are based on the three-digit subsectors of the 2022 North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) (Office of Management and Budget, 2022), with selected labels shortened for readability. (b): Source-engagement statistics summarize the financial value and human effort associated with the original client projects. (c): The benchmark covers six core OR expert capabilities reflected in the curated tasks. 3.2 Data Curation We curated 31 instances across 10 industrial scenarios from commissioned OR engagements. Experts with at least three years of professional OR experience de-identified the original requirements, input data, and deliverable formats while preserving the information boundary presented to the agent. They prepared the initial business brief and annotated the client-held facts that could be acquired through ORSIM. Detailed recruitment criteria and curation procedures are provided in Appendix G. Each instance provides the agent with the de-identified input files and initial brief. Hidden instancespecific verifiers and objective functions evaluate submitted decisions against the original operational requirements, while original expert solutions accepted by the clients provide the reference deliveries. Experts reviewed the consistency among the original project requirements, agent-facing materials, hidden evaluators, and reference solutions. The source engagements represent $3.68 million in total project value; problem sizes and additional engagement statistics are reported in Appendices and G.3. Figure 3 summarizes these engagement statistics. 3.3 ORSIM Real-world OR requirements are often incomplete at the start of project and may require clarification during formulation, solving, and refinement. We therefore introduce ORSIM, controlled client-interaction environment that exposes scenario-grounded client facts throughout the episode while withholding OR expertise. Each instance begins with an initial business brief and an expertreviewed catalog of client facts. The evaluated agent cannot inspect this catalog or the hidden evaluator. Only eligible client-owned facts can be disclosed, while problem formulation, algorithm selection, and solver implementation remain the agents responsibility. Each query can disclose at most three non-brief facts. For each question, simulator-side LLM selects relevant entries from the closed fact catalog. deterministic controller validates the selection and enforces the ownership, visibility, and per-query 5 OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners disclosure rules before passing the authorized text to response-only LLM for natural-language rendering. The selector and responder do not determine which information may be disclosed. This separation allows flexible semantic matching and language generation while keeping the information boundary programmatic. We evaluate ORSIM with expert-annotated reliability tests; the complete schema, selector variants, disclosure rules, and evaluation protocol are provided in Appendix C. 3.4 Metrics deployable OR solution must satisfy every operational constraint and attain competitive objective value. We therefore manually annotate three observable dimensions of each retained trajectory using task materials, interaction logs, execution feedback, and final artifacts. The complete coding and aggregation protocol is given in Appendix B. For client information acquisition, we assign each ask action to one of six OR workflow stages: before solver code (S1), before solver feedback (S2), before the first candidate (S3), before complete candidate (S4), before the self-check passes (S5), and before final submission (S6). We also record whether the agent asks again after solving feedback when another decision opportunity remains. For scientific inquiry, we annotate research opportunities: consequential uncertainties visible to the agent and potentially reducible through investigation. We report chain completion and, among opportunities with complete chain, stage quality based on three-level rubric. The rubric and aggregation rules are given in Appendix B. For trajectory-level error analysis, we identify confirmed error events from the agent trajectory and final artifact and classify each event by its point of origin. We use eight categories: problem understanding (UND), data and parameter mapping (DATA), decision representation (DEC), static constraints (CON), dynamic and state transitions (DYN), uncertainty and information structure (UNC), objective and preference formulation (OBJ), and implementation and delivery (IMP). Because trajectory may contain multiple error events, category profiles are computed at the event level, with infeasible rates reported separately.

sections.title: 4 Evaluation
sections.content: We evaluate eleven frontier models on the three research questions introduced in Section 1, with five runs per modeltask pair. Feasibility and DAQ first average the five runs within each task, then weight the 31 task means equally. Their reported spreads are the arithmetic means of the within-task sample standard deviations; conditional quality and its spread divide the DAQ mean and spread by the observed mean feasibility. These spreads describe within-task variation, not standard errors of the benchmark mean. Reliabilityquality profiles apply the same task-equal averaging to Z1/α before raising the result to α. We further analyze agents solution techniques, objective handling, and problem-structure exploitation in comparison with expert reference solutions in Appendix E. The complete model list, prompt templates, evaluation settings, and the average cost of each agent are provided in Appendix D. Execution setup. We use Claude Code as the primary evaluation harness and expose ORSIM through the Bash command ask. This provides common shell-based interface for model execution while keeping client interaction within the benchmark protocol. Complete model versions, execution budgets, prompts, and instance-specific settings are provided in Appendices and G. 4.1 RQ1: Cross-Model Comparison and Performance Against Human Experts Metric-based results. Table 1 shows that the models differ more in whether they complete feasible delivery than in their conditional objective quality. Feasibility spans 43.23 percentage points, from 45.16% for Hy3 to 88.39% for Grok 4.6, whereas conditional quality spans only 4.09 points, from 96.92% to 101.01%. These quality scores concern model-specific feasible subsets, however, and do not establish comparable optimization capability across all instances. Several models exceed the expert quality reference of 100% on their feasible deliveries, but DAQ places every model below the expert. Grok 4.6 achieves the highest DAQ in the primary comparison at 86.55%, leaving 13.45-point gap. Using DAQ = Feas Qfeas, this gap decomposes into 11.61 points from infeasible deliveries and 1.84 points from the net objective shortfall on feasible ones. Thus, approximately 86% of its score deficit comes from the zero credit assigned to failed deliveries. The dominant observed gap is therefore incomplete feasible delivery, rather than modest objective shortfalls on successful cases. The reliabilityquality profile in the right panel of Table 1 reinforces this distinction. Increasing α reduces the compensation that high-scoring instances provide for low-scoring or infeasible ones. All eleven models retain the same ranking across the 21 plotted values from 1 to 3, while their scores decrease and remain below the expert reference. The observed ordering is therefore stable across the tested reliability penalties, but no model closes the expert gap. Trajectory-based results. In particular, stopping at HCAE indicates that evidence has been interpreted without linked, evidence-grounded update. These are gaps in observable research-chain completion, not proof that every incomplete chain leaves its issue unsolved. Conditional stage quality and DAQ also yield different model rankings. GPT-5.6 Sol combines DAQ of 85.02% with relatively low conditional stage quality, whereas Qwen3.8-Max has the highest conditional stage quality but lower DAQ of 77.97%. Moreover, Qwen3.8-Max completes the chain in only 27% of research opportunities. High research quality within completed investigations does not imply that model can consistently sustain such investigations across research opportunities. These findings reveal key limitation of current agents: they can occasionally demonstrate strong evidence-based reasoning, but still lack the reliability to carry investigations from uncertainty to evidence-grounded revision throughout long-horizon OR problem solving. Final-delivery performance and sustained research capability therefore represent distinct dimensions of expertise that must be evaluated separately. 9 OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners 4.2 RQ2: Client Information Acquisition Across the OR Workflow The left panel of Figure 5 summarizes the timing and confirmed issue resolution of classifiable pre-submission client questions. We assign questions to S1S6 relative to solver-code development, observed feedback, candidate construction, self-checking, and final submission. Segment width denotes the task-equalized question share, and height the pooled confirmed-resolution proportion. Resolution requires concrete issue, targeted action, and confirming outcome; ordinary rule requests and unresolved or unknown outcomes remain in the denominator when their stage is known. Questioning is strongly front-loaded: S1 accounts for 86.7%98.3% of questions across models. Even for Hy4 Preview and GPT-5.6 Sol, only approximately 13% of questions occur after S1, compared with 9% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Later questions appear across different stages, including S3S5, but constitute small fraction of total interaction. Despite having access to client information throughout the workflow, agents predominantly treat information acquisition as an initial requirement-gathering activity, rather than consistently revisiting their understanding as solution development proceeds. Later-stage interactions nevertheless contribute to confirmed issue resolution. Confirmed-resolution proportions range from 10.6% to 37.0% in S1, compared with approximately 56% for DeepSeekV4.1-Flash in S4 and 71% for Hy4 Preview in S5. At S4, an initial candidate already exists; at S5, complete candidate has been constructed but has not yet passed self-checking. These observations show that client clarification can support the diagnosis and correction of concrete issues after solution construction has begun, rather than serving only to establish the initial specification. Taken together, these results reveal gap between continuous access to client information and its sustained use during problem solving. Agents can resolve specific issues through later clarification, yet their information-seeking behavior remains heavily concentrated before substantive solver development. key limitation of current agents is the lack of consistent, feedback-responsive process for identifying and resolving information gaps as solutions evolve. Reliable end-to-end OR agents should be able to recognize when intermediate results or execution feedback warrant revisiting business assumptions, seek targeted clarification, and incorporate the acquired facts into verified revisions of the formulation or implementation. 4.3 RQ3: LLM Failure Patterns in End-to-End OR Projects Within the annotated trajectories, formulation errors are prominent across models (Figure 5, right): implementation and delivery (IMP) is the largest error category for only two of the eleven models. Static constraint errors (CON) account for 42.7% of Claude Opus 5s error events, while dynamic and state-transition errors (DYN) account for 28.7% and 25.5% of those for Hy4 Preview and GLM5.3-Flash, respectively. Objective and preference formulation (OBJ) and uncertainty and information structure (UNC) together account for 69.0% of Grok 4.6s error events and 70.5% of Muse Spark 1.3s. These profiles identify what requires correction, rather than providing an additive attribution of each models failure probability. The distinction is between solving specified optimization problem and formulating the right problem from business requirements. An executable program may faithfully implement formulation that misrepresents the required objectives, state transitions, or information structure; improving execution alone would not correct that mismatch. Meanwhile, IMP remains the largest category for GPT-5.6 Sol and Hy3 (33.3% and 33.1%), so implementation failures also persist. Read alongside RQ1 and RQ2, these findings motivate agents that use both experimental evidence and client facts to revisit their task interpretation and revise the adopted solution. The central requirement is not merely runnable code or plausible numerical outputs, but consistency from business semantics through formulation, implementation, and validation. 10 OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: OR-LICENSE evaluates LLM agents on 31 de-identified OR instances from 10 industrial scenarios using original client materials, ORSIM-mediated interaction, hidden feasibility checks, and client-accepted expert references. Across eleven evaluated models, several exceed the expertnormalized objective-quality reference on feasible instances, yet none matches the expert reference in Deployment-Adjusted Quality. Trajectory analysis shows that information acquisition continues beyond initial clarification into solution development and validation; for some models, later-stage questions are associated with higher confirmed issue-resolution proportions. These findings motivate better requirement interpretation, formulation, validation, sustained information-gap resolution, and evidence-linked self-improvement. 11 OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners AI Use Statement We used generative AI tools to assist with translation, dataset cleaning and reformatting, qualitative and thematic data analysis, scientific figure presentation, manuscript editing, software development, and literature discovery. sections.content: This appendix specifies the coding and aggregation rules summarized in Section 3.5. 18 OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners Client information acquisition. Motivated by the information-value view of clarification questions (Rao & Daumé III, 2018), we examine when agents ask questions throughout the solution workflow. We assign each ask action to one of six event-based stages according to when the question is issued: S1 (before solver code), before the agent first writes substantive code for solving the task; S2 (before solver feedback), after solver-code development begins but before the agent observes the first feedback from solving attempt; S3 (before the first candidate), after observing this feedback but before producing the first inspectable candidate containing concrete business decisions; S4 (before complete candidate), after the first candidate appears but before candidate covers the full required decision scope; S5 (before passing self-checks), after complete candidate is available but before the agents own checks report that it passes; and S6 (before final submission), after passing these self-checks but before final submission. Self-checks are checks performed by the agent during the trajectory before final submission. We also record whether an agent asks again after observing solver feedback, conditional on having further decision opportunity. Trajectory error analysis. Guided by the OR problem-solving workflow (Hillier et al., 1995) and prior work on optimization agents (AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024), we identify confirmed error events in each agent trajectory and final artifact and classify each event by its point of origin. We use eight categories: problem understanding (UND), data and parameter mapping (DATA), decision representation (DEC), static constraints (CON), dynamic and state transitions (DYN), uncertainty and information structure (UNC), objective and preference formulation (OBJ), and implementation and delivery (IMP). Because trajectory may contain multiple error events, category profiles are computed at the event level, with infeasible rates reported separately. Simulator or infrastructure failures are recorded separately and are not attributed to the agent. Scientific inquiry. Drawing on hypothesisexperiment coordination (Klahr & Dunbar, 1988) and inquiry cycles (Pedaste et al., 2015), we analyze research opportunities within agent trajectories. research opportunity is consequential uncertainty visible to the agent and potentially reducible through investigation, such as unexpected infeasibility, unexplained objective deterioration, or an untested modeling assumption. Competing explanations and repeated experiments addressing the same uncertainty belong to one opportunity. Domain experts first enumerate research opportunities from each full recorded trajectory, then annotate stage presence, stage quality, and chain completion for each opportunity using the fixed inventory. Stage presence and chain completion. For each opportunity, we independently annotate testable hypothesis (H), mechanistic explanation (C), an executed diagnostic experiment (A), interpretation of the resulting evidence (E), and an actual evidence-grounded update (U). sections.title: C Details and Reliability of ORSIM
sections.content: ORSIM simulates business client during an OR engagement. This appendix describes its design and evaluates its reliability. C.1 Simulator Architecture and Selector Variants Design motivation. To reduce hallucinations in client interactions, we separate evidence selection from response generation. Prior work has explored several complementary mechanisms for interactive information elicitation. Abdullin et al. (2025) condition simulated user on the complete problem statement and introduce comparison-based feedback to correct the modeling agents summaries. AgentMILO (Gaddam et al., 2025) uses expert-designed knowledge graphs to guide the modeling agents questions and mathematical formulations. The Human Imitator (Duan et al., 2025) is fine-tuned to reproduce ambiguity and bounded rationality in managerial dialogue, while τRec (Narasimhan & Narasimhan, 2026) assigns disclosure tags to private user constraints. Our focus is faithful, controlled disclosure of instance-specific business knowledge: the evidence supporting each simulated client reply is explicitly identified before the reply is generated. Selectorresponder architecture. We first decompose the complete client-side problem statement into catalog of business rules, each associated with stable identifier. Given an agents question, simulator-side LLM selects relevant rule identifiers for evidence retrieval. deterministic controller validates these identifiers and applies the disclosure policy before passing the authorized rule texts to the responder. The responder is instructed to render only the authorized business facts in natural language and to identify any parts of the question that this evidence leaves unresolved. The complete rule catalog remains hidden from the evaluated agent. The selected identifiers make the factual basis of each reply explicit and inspectable. Ledger schema and disclosure policy. Each ledger entry has stable fact_id, one or more sourcegrounded answer units, knowledge_owner label, an in_brief flag, and optional links to verifier rules or objective components. The owner label distinguishes client facts from information assigned OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners to the input data, an external system, or OR expertise. For each query, the deterministic controller accepts only identifiers that satisfy the ownership and visibility policy. In the benchmark condition, it allows at most three newly disclosed non-brief client facts per query; facts already present in the initial brief may be restated but do not count as newly disclosed. Requests for input-data, external-system, or OR-expertise information receive fixed role-specific refusals. The response-only model receives only the authorized source text, and failed or unsafe rendering falls back to that text. Neither the evaluated agent nor the response model can inspect the complete ledger or hidden evaluator state. Selector representations. Related work on evidence-grounded generation has explored finegrained propositions (Chen et al., 2024), hierarchical summaries (Sarthi et al., 2024), and knowledge graphs with community summaries (Edge et al., 2024). However, advances in long-context processing also motivate direct access to complete source information when the knowledge base fits within the available context budget (Li et al., 2024; Chan et al., 2025). In our setting, this raises the question of whether an LLM can select relevant rules more reliably from their full texts than from additional summary or graph representations. Direct access may preserve conditions and exceptions that intermediate representations omit, while structured representations may make relevant information easier to locate. We therefore investigate three selector designs: (1) Flat selector. The selector receives the question together with the complete catalog of rule identifiers and full rule texts. It directly selects the identifiers needed to answer the question, without an intermediate summary index or knowledge graph. All candidate rules are available for joint consideration in single selection step, including details whose relevance becomes apparent only in relation to other rules. (2) Summary-plus-detail selector. Concise summaries provide an index for locating relevant rules, while the corresponding full rule texts provide the evidence for response generation. The selector uses the summaries to identify relevant content and retrieves the associated details. This reduces the amount of text used for initial selection, but may overlook rules whose relevance depends on conditions or exceptions omitted from their summaries. (3) Summary-plus-KG selector. textual overview provides global context, while knowledge graph organizes business entities and their relations. The selector uses both representations to identify relevant knowledge and select the associated business-rule texts as answer evidence. This design makes relational structure explicit, but introduces additional opportunities for information loss or distortion during graph construction and graph-based selection. We ultimately adopt the flat selector as the default implementation. It keeps the complete rule details available during selection while avoiding intermediate summary-based filtering or graph construction. Crucially, access to the full catalog is limited to the selection stage: the responder still receives only selected, authorized evidence. We evaluate the resulting simulators reliability below. C.2 Reliability Analysis We evaluate the simulator at two levels: whether the selector identifies the business rules needed to answer question, and whether the resulting reply faithfully satisfies the reference requirements while respecting the clients information boundary. We also examine consistency across repeated runs, since occasional unsupported or incomplete replies can introduce noise into the evaluation of the optimization agent. Response-level metrics are derived from shared set of component annotations, whose interannotator agreement is assessed separately. Evaluation setup. We construct an expert-annotated evaluation set containing 204 queries across 5 benchmark instances. The set includes 119 standard queries and 85 adversarial queries. Standard queries cover individual business rules, questions requiring multiple rules, and conditions or exceptions that must be preserved in the answer. Adversarial queries probe unsupported assumptions, OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners requests to invent missing information, and attempts to obtain information or OR advice outside the simulated clients role. For each query, domain experts annotate the relevant, disclosable business-rule identifiers and the expected response requirements. These specify both the information that should be conveyed and any required correction, acknowledgment of insufficient information, or refusal. Questions that depend on earlier exchanges are paired with fixed dialogue history and disclosure state. The reference annotations are shared across selector variants but are not available to the simulator. Compared variants. We compare the flat, summary-plus-detail, and summary-plus-KG selectors described in Section C.1. All three selector variants use the same underlying business-rule catalog, disclosure policy, and responder. We hold the selector backbone, responder backbone, and decoding settings fixed, so that the comparison isolates the effect of the selector representation and selection procedure. The simulator uses DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Each query is evaluated in 5 independent runs per selector variant, with its initial dialogue history and disclosure state restored before every run. This produces 204 3 5 = 3,060 replies. Each selector variant therefore contributes 119 5 = 595 replies to standard queries and 85 5 = 425 replies to adversarial queries. Full-statement direct-answer baseline. We additionally include an end-to-end baseline in which the responder uses the complete problem statement as evidence to answer the query directly. We match the responder backbone, decoding settings, fixed dialogue context, and disclosure policy across configurations. This comparison characterizes the end-to-end configurations, jointly varying source representation and evidence provision. The full-statement results cover 204 5 = 1,020 replies, with the same split of 119 standard and 85 adversarial queries and five runs per query. D.2 Models We evaluate the eleven models listed in Table 1: Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026), DeepSeek-V4.1Flash (DeepSeek, 2026), Gemini 3.8 Flash (Google, 2026), GLM-5.3-Flash (Z.AI, 2026), Grok 4.6 (xAI, 2026), GPT-5.6 Sol (OpenAI, 2026a), Hy3 (Tencent, 2026a), Hy4 preview (Tencent, 2026b), Muse Spark 1.3 (Meta, 2026), Qwen3.8-Max (Alibaba Group, 2026), and Doubao-Seed-2.1-Pro (ByteDance Seed Team, 2026). D.3 Settings We use Harbor 0.18.0 as the execution framework. The harness versions used in our experiments are Claude Code 2.1.278 and Codex 0.155.1. The interaction policy imposes hard maximum of 500 rounds. Harbor-native tasks are allocated 12-hour (43,200-s) wall-clock budget, and each solver invocation is limited to 3,600 s, including the solver subprocess and feedback paths. These values are upper bounds; an episode may terminate earlier after successful completion or verification. Table 5 records the model-level decoding settings requested for the model labels listed in Table 1. Max context denotes the effective context cap enforced by the gateway, and thinking strength denotes the request-level reasoning control. D.4 Semantic Validation Bike-sharing Tasks 2631 require additional semantic validation due to their specialized modeling requirements involving scenario structures, risk preferences, and rolling optimization. These requirements concern not only the feasibility and objective quality of final decisions, but also whether the underlying solver correctly implements the prescribed optimization formulations and decision processes, which cannot be fully verified through deterministic checks alone. 27 OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners For these tasks, all results reported in this paper were manually reviewed by human experts. To facilitate community use, we also provide human-validated LLM-as-a-judge protocol for this semantic review. The recorded judge configuration specifies DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, maximum output length of 393,216 tokens, and high reasoning strength. To validate this protocol, each task was judged five times, and every judgment was independently checked by two human experts. All judgments agreed with both human assessments, supporting the reliability of this configuration within our evaluation setting. The prompts are presented in Appendix D.5. Solution Strategies and Optimization-Structure Exploitation To characterize how LLMs select and organize optimization methods, we annotate the final adopted solution strategy along three dimensions: solution techniques (T), objective handling (O), and problem-structure exploitation (S). Annotations concern the final submitted program and the computational workflow that produces the submitted solution. Abandoned approaches and unused code are excluded, and default mechanisms internal to solver are not attributed as additional agent-designed methods. The three dimensions characterize algorithm and tool use, objective design, and the recognition and exploitation of optimization structure, respectively. E.1 Annotation Framework Solution techniques (T). This dimension identifies the algorithmic mechanisms used to generate decisions. We distinguish seven categories: general-purpose optimization solver invocation (T1), specialized structural algorithms or analytical methods (T2), greedy or rule-based construction (T3), local or neighborhood search (T4), metaheuristics or randomized optimization (T5), enumeration (T6), and branching search (T7). T6 covers explicit generation and evaluation or filtering of finite collection of candidates. T7 covers an explicitly controlled tree of partial decisions in which branches are expanded and excluded. Branch-and-bound, pruning, and heuristics performed internally by general-purpose solver are subsumed under T1. hybrid strategy may receive multiple labels when distinct modules participate in the adopted workflow. Operations within single complete algorithm are not counted repeatedly; for example, neighborhood moves internal to metaheuristic do not independently receive T4. Objective handling (O). This dimension identifies the criterion guiding decisions at the level of the overall task. We assign one of two mutually exclusive labels: direct business-objective handling (O1) or autonomous surrogate-objective handling (O2). O1 covers direct optimization of the prescribed business objectives and equivalent treatments that preserve their priority relationships, including optimization of prescribed secondary objective within the primary-optimal solution set. O2 covers independently designed scores, weights, or local subobjectives that substitute for the complete business objective to guide construction or staged optimization. The absence of an explicit mathematical objective in the problem statement does not by itself imply O2: faithfully translating 41 OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners business requirement into mathematical expression remains O1. The labels depend on the criterion governing solution selection and are independent of whether the agent or expert wrote the objective expression. Problem-structure exploitation (S). This dimension identifies structural properties actively exploited to organize, simplify, or restrict optimization. We distinguish four categories: equivalent compression and reformulation (S1), autonomous decomposition (S2), specialized structural algorithm exploitation (S3), and valid tightening or search-space reduction (S4). S1 includes justified aggregation, variable elimination, and compact equivalent representations of models or objectives. S2 includes autonomously chosen rolling schemes, task or resource decomposition, and state propagation or coordination between subproblems. S3 requires identifying an applicable matching, network-flow, dynamic-programming, or other specialized structure and actually using the corresponding algorithm. S4 covers valid bounds, dominance relations, symmetry reduction, or objective-value restrictions used to narrow subsequent search. Merely implementing explicitly required multiple periods, scenarios, or decision rounds does not qualify as additional structural exploitation. Multiple distinct structural operations may receive multiple labels. Relationships between the dimensions. The three dimensions describe different aspects of strategy and can jointly characterize the same workflow. For example, an autonomously designed rolling scheduling strategy receives S2 when it divides the planning task into successive subproblems and propagates state between them. Within each window, decisions may be generated by an optimization solver or by rule-based construction, corresponding to T1 or T3. The window-level criterion may preserve the prescribed business objective or replace it with an independently designed guidance score, corresponding to O1 or O2. Rolling execution alone therefore determines neither the technique label nor the objective-handling label. As second example, consider strategy that first establishes the primary optimum, then adds constraint preserving that value and solves second model for the prescribed secondary objective. This strategy can receive T1, O1, and S4: T1 records solver invocation, O1 records preservation of the prescribed objective hierarchy, and S4 records the use of the primary optimum to restrict subsequent optimization. The labels describe strategies and their combinations; adoption frequency itself is not score of method quality. Aggregate agent rates weight tasks equally within each model and then average equally across models. The results show that LLMs can combine optimization tools, candidate construction, and search procedures, while their differences from the expert extend to how these mechanisms connect objectives with problem structure. From tool invocation to method composition. As shown in Figure 6, agents invoke generalpurpose optimization solvers (T1) in 78.0% of tasks, compared with 93.5% for the expert. Conversely, greedy or rule-based construction (T3) is more frequent among agents (29.6%) than in the expert solutions (19.4%). General-purpose solvers are therefore central component of LLM-generated solutions, alongside procedures that construct decisions through successive selection, assignment, or ordering. These techniques can contribute jointly to the final solution: an agent may construct candidates before selecting among them with solver, or adjust an initial solver-generated solution. Tool-use capability thus includes composing methods into an executable solution process, beyond invoking an optimization library. Instance-specific methods and paths to scalability. Explicit enumeration (T6) appears in 12.3% of agent solutions, compared with 3.2% of expert solutions. In the trajectories, enumeration is mainly used to generate local feasible combinations, construct batch or wave catalogs, and compare finite parameter configurations, followed by selection through solver or an evaluation rule. These 42 OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners Figure 6: Solution-technique adoption across LLMs and the expert reference. Rows represent models and the expert; columns represent categories T1T7. Each cell reports the percentage of the 31 tasks receiving that label, using one selected solution scheme per modeltask pair. Labels may coexist, so row percentages need not sum to 100%. Color intensity indicates adoption rate on 0100% scale. approaches demonstrate the ability to devise direct methods for the current instance: when the candidate space is manageable, explicit generation and comparison provide clear and readily implementable solution procedure. The computational demands of such procedures depend strongly on the size of the candidate space. Combinatorial enumeration can grow exponentially, and even enumeration of fixed-size combinations can produce rapidly expanding candidate catalogs. Some expert solutions instead use rule-based construction, neighborhood improvement, or coordinated decomposition to generate and improve solutions progressively, with adjustable iteration budgets, neighborhood sizes, or search effort. The contrast reveals different design tendencies: agents more frequently handle candidates explicitly for the current instance, whereas expert solutions more often retain iterative mechanisms that offer paths for accommodating larger problems. Reformulating representations and organizing structured search. Figure 7 shows that equivalent compression and reformulation (S1) are more frequent among agents (13.2%) than in the expert solutions (6.5%). Autonomous decomposition (S2) and valid tightening or search-space reduction (S4), by contrast, are less frequent among agents: 23.2% and 27.3%, respectively, compared with 41.9% and 45.2% for the expert. Agents often use aggregation, precomputation, and compact representations to transform problem into form suitable for subsequent optimization. The expert more frequently organizes the solution process through rolling windows, subproblem partitioning, state propagation, and valid bounds. Both exploit problem structure, but at different points in the solution process: agent strategies more often emphasize representation changes, while expert strategies more often use structure OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners Figure 7: Objective handling (a) and problem-structure exploitation (b) across LLMs and the expert reference. Both panels use 0100% color scale. throughout the organization of search. Agent use of S1 is also concentrated across tasks: Tasks 12 and 30 account for 44.4% of all positive S1 annotations. This concentration indicates consistent treatment of particular structures rather than uniform tendency across problem types. Tool use and objective design are distinct capabilities. Agents use autonomous surrogate objectives (O2) in 26.4% of tasks, compared with 38.7% for the expert. Among the experts O2 solutions, 83.3% also invoke general-purpose solver. Meanwhile, 49.5% of agent solutions using greedy or rule-based construction retain the direct business objective (O1). Solution techniques and objective handling therefore do not have one-to-one correspondence. The expert may optimize self-designed local score or surrogate objective with solver to guide complex decisions. Agents may also generate candidates through rules and then select among them using the full business objective. These combinations distinguish the ability to use optimization tools from the ability to design optimization guidance and preserve the business evaluation criterion. The higher agent adoption of O1 reflects greater tendency to retain direct business evaluation, whereas the higher expert adoption of O2 reflects more frequent use of autonomous objective design to organize local or staged optimization. Different models emphasize different capabilities. Across models, general-purpose solver adoption ranges from 67.7% to 87.1%, surrogate-objective adoption from 16.1% to 48.4%, and tightening or search-space reduction from 9.7% to 41.9%. The model whose adoption rate is closest to the expert also varies by dimension. Doubao-Seed-2.1-Pro and Qwen3.8-Max both invoke solvers in 44 OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners 87.1% of tasks, closest to the experts 93.5%. Gemini 3.8 Flash uses surrogate objectives in 35.5% of tasks, close to the experts 38.7%. Grok 4.6 has the closest autonomous-decomposition rate (35.5%, compared with 41.9%), while GLM-5.3-Flash has the closest tightening and search-reduction rate (41.9%, compared with 45.2%). These profiles show that frequent solver use does not necessarily coincide with frequent autonomous objective design or structured search. The joint TOS analysis exposes differences that single tool-invocation rate cannot capture: LLMs demonstrate capabilities in devising instance-specific methods and reformulating problem representations, while connecting objective design, subproblem organization, and search control into complete solution process remains deeper distinction from the expert reference solutions.

sections.title: F Extended Comparison with Related Benchmarks
sections.content: This appendix expands the comparison across benchmarks for operations research (OR), combinatorial optimization, and professional work. Table 8 compares task and data sources, preservation of original client materials, multi-step agent evaluation, the nature of client interaction, and the provenance of reference solutions. Optimization modeling and constraint reasoning. major line of work evaluates the ability to translate prepared problem descriptions into optimization models or solve explicitly specified optimization tasks. NL4Opt uses annotated linear-programming word problems (Ramamonjison et al., 2023), while Mamo draws on academic materials (Huang et al., 2024) and OptiBench collects problems from textbooks, assignments, and examinations (Yang et al., 2025). IndustryOR brings industrial content into this setting through abstracted industrial optimization problems (Huang et al., 2025). Complementing these sources, OptMATH-Bench uses bidirectional data synthesis (Lu et al., 2025), and ConstraintBench constructs synthetic OR scenarios for evaluating constraint reasoning (Tso et al., 2026). These benchmarks support systematic evaluation of modeling and reasoning under prepared task specification, centering on the accurate encoding of supplied requirements. OR-LICENSE starts from original business requirements and input formats preserved through de-identification, with partial requirements disclosed in the initial brief. Agents establish the relevant specification by acquiring additional client-held facts and integrating them into the development of an executable solution. This setting evaluates requirement acquisition, interpretation, and formalization together with solver development. Combinatorial optimization and algorithm engineering. Another line of evaluation emphasizes computational problem solving and the development of effective algorithms. GraphArena evaluates graph computation using public graph datasets (Tang et al., 2025). Agent-oriented benchmarks extend evaluation to algorithm search and implementation: CO-Bench draws on OR-Library and the optimization literature (Sun et al., 2026); RoutBench, introduced with ARS, uses synthetic vehiclerouting variants (Li et al., 2025); HeuriGym draws on open-source projects and research papers to evaluate LLM-crafted heuristics (Chen et al., 2025); and ALE-Bench uses AtCoder Heuristic Contest problems for long-horizon, objective-driven algorithm engineering (Imajuku et al., 2025). These agent-oriented benchmarks evaluate multi-step work and executable outcomes for specified optimization tasks. Their central challenge is selecting, implementing, and refining methods that produce competitive solutions from supplied task definitions. OR-LICENSE combines this algorithmic work with the acquisition and interpretation of client requirements. The resulting evaluation covers both establishing the optimization task and developing solution that satisfies its operational constraints and achieves competitive objective quality. Multi-stage OR agent benchmarks. OR-Space and ORAgentBench are particularly close to our setting because they broaden OR evaluation to executable environments and multi-stage agent workflows. OR-Space reconstructs IndustryOR problems as multi-file workspaces (Zhou et al., 2026). These environments evaluate agents that inspect task assets, implement solutions, and complete several stages of optimization. OR-LICENSE uses original client materials as the starting point for this workflow. Agents can elicit missing business facts as information needs arise during formulation, solving, and refinement, and their final deliveries are compared with client-accepted expert references from the original engagements. This connects multi-stage agent evaluation to the requirements, information boundaries, and completed deliveries of the source projects. Professional-work and long-horizon agent benchmarks. Beyond OR, recent benchmarks make completed professional work products and sustained execution central units of evaluation. GDPval uses professional work products adapted by experts (Patwardhan et al., 2025), APEX-Agents provides expert-constructed professional workspaces (Vidgen et al., 2026), and AgencyBench curates tasks from real-world AI usage and includes rubric-based feedback (Li et al., 2026b). Their empha46 OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners sis on completed deliverables and sustained execution provides broader context for evaluating economically relevant work. OR-LICENSE specializes this direction to OR deliveries, where an executable decision must satisfy operational constraints before its objective quality can be meaningfully assessed. Our construction links each evaluated delivery to the original client requirements, the information available during the engagement, and the expert solution ultimately accepted by the client. Client interaction as information acquisition. The client-interaction column characterizes how agents receive task-relevant information during an episode. File inspection gives access to supplied materials, and solver feedback reports computational outcomes under the agents current formulation. ORAgentBench supplies scripted event updates (Li et al., 2026a), while AgencyBench supports deliverable revision through rubric-based feedback (Li et al., 2026b). Interactive user simulation appears in customer-service settings such as τ-bench (Yao et al., 2024), and elicitation has been studied in optimization modeling dialogues (Abdullin et al., 2025); OR-LICENSE differs by tying elicited business facts to executable optimization deliverables. Client fact elicitation evaluates how agents identify missing business requirements, formulate questions, and incorporate the resulting answers into their solutions. GDPval explicitly acknowledges that supplying the full task context leaves out the work required to establish that context (Patwardhan et al., 2025). In OR-LICENSE, agents receive an initial business brief and the task input files, while additional client-held facts are accessible through ORSIM. Client interaction remains available throughout formulation, solving, and refinement, allowing agents to revisit requirements as new information needs arise. The simulated client provides authorized business facts; the agent is responsible for mathematical formulations and algorithmic choices. This design makes identifying information gaps, asking relevant questions, and incorporating the answers part of the same optimization episode, with explicit responsibilities for the client and the OR agent. Original materials and client-accepted reference solutions. The comparison tracks the provenance of both task inputs and reference solutions. The original client materials criterion requires original project requirements and inputs preserved through de-identification only. The client-accepted references criterion requires that reference solutions were accepted in the original professional engagements before benchmark construction. OR-LICENSE uses original expert solutions produced in paid, competitively awarded OR engagements and accepted by clients before the benchmark was constructed. Hidden evaluation checks feasibility and compares agent and expert objective quality under the same instance-specific criteria. The reference anchors evaluation to an achieved professional outcome, and agents can pursue their own formulations and solution methods. An agent that produces feasible solution with better objective value receives expert-relative quality above one. OR-LICENSE combines original industrial materials, client fact elicitation throughout optimization, and reference deliveries accepted before benchmark construction, supporting evaluation of the complete path from understanding an unfamiliar business setting to producing an executable, feasible, and competitively optimized decision.

sections.title: G Dataset Details
sections.content: G.1 Expert Recruitment and Task Construction Expert recruitment. We recruited contributors with substantial professional operations research experience to provide source projects and curate them into benchmark instances. Each expert held masters degree or higher in industrial engineering and operations research, computer science, electrical engineering, or data science, and had at least three years of professional OR experience. Experts were compensated at rates commensurate with their time commitment and level of expertise. Project selection and de-identification. We selected representative projects from professional OR practice. For each project, domain experts de-identified the original requirements, data, and 47 OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners deliverable materials and prepared brief.md file containing the business background disclosed to the agent at the start of evaluation. The agent-facing package retains the associated de-identified input files. Experts also annotated the client-held information that could be acquired through ORSIM during formulation, solving, and refinement. The initial brief, input files, and authorized client disclosures therefore define the information available to the agent during an episode. Evaluation artifacts and reference solutions. For each instance, experts supplied hidden constraintchecking verifiers and objective-function specifications. These artifacts reconstruct the task-specific operational requirements and remain unavailable to the agent during execution. We retained the original expert solution and the original client requirements as source materials for construction and validation. The reference solutions were produced in commissioned, competitively awarded OR engagements and accepted by the clients before benchmark construction. Further checks of the executable reference code, hidden evaluators, and preserved information boundary are described in the next subsection. Coverage and source engagements. The resulting dataset contains 31 instances spanning 10 industrial scenarios. All source materials were cleared for benchmark use and were preserved after de-identification without recasting the requirements as complete mathematical formulations. The source engagements represent $3.68 million in total project value, with an average duration of 4.7 months and 2.16 experts per project. Problem-size estimates are reported in Appendix G.3. G.2 Task Quality Control Experts independently reviewed each instance. They verified that the human-authored solution code executed correctly and that the hidden constraint checker and objective function implemented the original business rules and evaluation criteria. They compared the initial brief and input files with the original project records to confirm that de-identification preserved the original information boundaries, ambiguity, and business terminology. The initial brief retained the business requirements without recasting them as complete mathematical formulation. It excluded facts that required client interaction, which remained accessible through ORSIM, as well as structural insights and other knowledge acquired during subsequent expert analysis. G.3 Problem Sizes Table 9 reports approximate model-size estimates derived from each tasks conditions and implementation. These estimates summarize the potential scale of decision variables and constraints across tasks. G.4 Verification, Evaluation, and Competency Coverage Each benchmark instance is evaluated in two logically separate stages.
